Chapter Two: Building Trust and Character as the Foundation
Once you really grasp how important influence is, the next thing you need to realize is this: trust and character are the soil where true influence takes root. Without a strong base of integrity, any effort to lead others—no matter how well-intentioned—will eventually crumble.
Think of trust like building a stone wall, one brick at a time. Every honest action, every promise you keep, each moment of transparency—they all add strength to that wall. But here’s the tough part: a single act of dishonesty or betrayal can bring it all tumbling down, wiping away years of effort in just an instant.
What are the core elements that make up trust in leadership? Well, for starters:
Consistency. People need to know what to expect from their leaders. When your behavior is steady and predictable, it creates a sense of safety and reliability.
Honesty. Telling the truth—even when it’s uncomfortable—shows respect for others and a real commitment to doing the right thing.
And accountability. Owning your mistakes and taking responsibility, instead of shifting blame, is what truly builds credibility.
Picture a manager who always follows through on their word, admits when they’re wrong, and treats everyone fairly. Over time, their team learns they can count on this person, even when the going gets tough. That trust becomes a powerful glue, helping the group take risks, try new things, and stick together through setbacks.
On the flip side, imagine a leader who cuts corners, hides their mistakes, or plays favorites. Trust erodes fast, and when it’s gone, it’s really hard—sometimes impossible—to get it back.
Now, let’s dig a bit deeper. Character is the invisible framework that supports trust. It doesn’t show up in grand gestures, but in everyday choices: how you treat a colleague who’s struggling, how you react to criticism, and how you behave when nobody’s watching.
The real test of a leader’s character comes during tough times. When resources are tight, when the path forward isn’t clear, or when mistakes happen, people are watching—looking for cues. Will you stay true to your values, or compromise for a quick win?
So, how do you actually build trust and character?
Start by keeping your promises, even the small ones. Be open about your intentions and decisions. Treat everyone with respect, no matter their title. And stand up for what’s right, even if it isn’t popular.
Practicing these habits, day in and day out, fills up a reservoir of goodwill you can tap into when challenges come your way. Even more, it sets the tone for your whole organization, showing everyone that integrity isn’t just a nice-to-have—it’s absolutely essential.
In the end, trust and character aren’t just about personal virtue—they’re strategic assets. They let you inspire loyalty, spark real collaboration, and create an environment where people can truly do their best work.
